sentences.text: Just as stunt doubles replace actors in dangerous scenes, test doubles replace real objects in tests.

sentences.text: But not all test doubles are created equal—mocks, stubs, fakes, and spies serve different purposes and follow different patterns.↵Understanding these distinctions transforms how you write tests.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: This guide clarifies what each test double does, when to use it, and how to implement it effectively.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Gerard Meszaros introduced the term "test double" in his book "xUnit Test Patterns" as an umbrella term for any object that replaces a real dependency in tests.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Martin Fowler popularized these concepts, particularly the distinction between mocks and stubs.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Test doubles fall into five categories, each with distinct characteristics:↵**Dummy**: Passed around but never used (fills parameter lists)↵**Stub**: Provides predefined responses to calls↵**Spy**: Records information about how it was called↵**Mock**: Verifies behavior with expectations↵**Fake**: Working implementation with shortcuts↵This guide focuses on the four most commonly used types: Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Stubs provide predefined answers to calls made during tests.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: They don't care how they're called—they simply return configured responses.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Stubs enable state verification: "Given this input, does the system produce the correct output?"

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Returns hardcoded responses↵No verification of how it's called↵Focuses on state verification↵Simplest form of test double

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Use stubs when you need to control what a dependency returns:↵Testing different response scenarios↵Simulating error conditions↵Providing test data↵Replacing slow operations (database queries, API calls)

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Mocks are test doubles with expectations about how they should be called.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Unlike stubs, which focus on what they return, mocks focus on how they're used.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Mocks enable behavior verification: "Was this method called with the correct parameters?"

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Verifies method calls and parameters↵Fails test if expectations not met↵Focuses on behavior verification↵More complex than stubs

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Use mocks when the interaction itself is what you're testing:↵Verifying a method was called↵Checking call order↵Validating parameters passed↵Ensuring correct number of calls

sentences.text: Prefer state verification (stubs) when possible.

sentences.text: Fakes are working implementations that take shortcuts unsuitable for production.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: They behave like real objects but use simpler, faster approaches.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Fakes are more complex than stubs but provide more realistic behavior.

sentences.text: Use fakes when you need realistic behavior without production complexity:↵In-memory database for testing↵Local file system instead of cloud storage↵Simplified authentication↵Fast alternatives to slow operations

sentences.text: Spies wrap real objects, recording how they're called while delegating to the actual implementation.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: They combine real behavior with verification capabilities, enabling observation without replacement.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Wraps real object↵Delegates to actual implementation↵Records all interactions↵Enables verification of real behavior

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Use spies when you need to verify interactions with real objects:↵Verifying caching behavior↵Checking optimization (method called fewer times)↵Monitoring real object usage↵Partial mocking (spy some methods, real others)

sentences.text: Spies can selectively override methods while keeping others real:↵ ↵:::warning{title="Spy Limitations"}↵**When spies don't work well:**↵Real object has side effects (sends emails, charges cards)↵Real object is slow (database queries, API calls)↵Real object requires complex setup↵Testing error conditions (real object doesn't fail on demand)↵**Solution:** Use mocks or stubs instead when real behavior is problematic.↵:::

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Selecting the appropriate test double depends on what you're testing and what you need to verify.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: | Aspect | Stub | Mock | Fake | Spy |↵|--------|------|------|------|-----|↵| **Complexity** | Low | Medium | High | Low |↵| **Verifies calls** | No | Yes | No | Yes |↵| **Real implementation** | No | No | Simplified | Yes |↵| **Maintains state** | No | No | Yes | Yes (real) |↵| **Setup effort** | Minimal | Medium | High | Minimal |↵| **Test clarity** | High | Medium | High | Medium |↵| **Brittleness** | Low | High | Low | Medium |

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: :::anote{title="When to Use Each Type"}↵**Use Stub when:**↵You need to control return values↵Testing different scenarios (success, failure)↵Replacing slow operations↵State verification is sufficient↵**Use Mock when:**↵Verifying method was called↵Checking parameters passed↵Validating call order↵Interaction is what matters↵**Use Fake when:**↵Need realistic behavior↵Testing complex interactions↵State persists across operations↵Real implementation too slow/complex↵**Use Spy when:**↵Need real behavior↵Want to verify optimization↵Partial mocking needed↵Monitoring real object usage↵:::

sentences.text: **Problem:** Mocking everything, including simple objects.↵

sentences.text: Follow these practices to write effective tests with test doubles.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: State verification (using stubs) is less brittle than behavior verification (using mocks).

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Test what the system produces, not how it produces it.↵

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Complex test doubles indicate design problems.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: If a test double is hard to create, the real object is probably too complex.↵

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Use descriptive names that indicate the double's purpose.↵

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Test doubles are essential tools for writing effective unit tests.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Understanding the distinctions between mocks, stubs, fakes, and spies enables you to choose the right tool for each testing scenario.↵**Key takeaways:**↵**Stubs** control outputs—use for state verification↵**Mocks** verify behavior—use sparingly at architectural boundaries↵**Fakes** provide working implementations—use for complex dependencies↵**Spies** observe real objects—use when real behavior matters↵ ↵The best tests use the simplest test double that meets their needs.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Prefer stubs over mocks, real objects over test doubles, and state verification over behavior verification.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Mock at architectural boundaries, not internal implementation details.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Keep test doubles simple—complex doubles indicate design problems.↵Master these patterns, and your tests become clearer, more maintainable, and more valuable.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: They'll catch bugs without breaking during refactoring, communicate intent without obscuring logic, and run fast without sacrificing confidence.↵Test doubles aren't just testing tools—they're design feedback mechanisms.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Difficulty creating test doubles reveals design problems: too many dependencies, unclear boundaries, or excessive coupling.

sourceRef.title: Test Doubles: Understanding Mock, Stub, Fake, and Spy

sentences.text: Listen to this feedback, and your code will become more modular, testable, and maintainable.↵Start applying these patterns today.
